summary: This informational document summarizes operational implications of the IPv6 extension headers in RFC 8200 and analyzes why packets with them are often dropped on the public Internet.

eli5.summary: IPv6 packets can carry extra labels, but many network devices throw those packets away. This document explains the reasons for that.

questions: why are ipv6 extension headers dropped
how do routers handle ipv6 packets with extension headers
why do firewalls filter ipv6 extension headers
subtitle: Why network devices often drop IPv6 packets with extra headers

tldr.problem: IPv6 extension headers allow the protocol to carry extra information like fragmentation data, but many routers and network devices intentionally drop packets containing them.
tldr.mechanism: Modern routers have hardware limitations that make processing extension headers expensive or impossible. Networks also drop them to enforce security policies, avoid performance hits, and work around bugs in device implementations.
tldr.outcome: IPv6 extension headers remain poorly supported in practice despite being part of the IPv6 specification, limiting their usefulness for new protocol features.

today: RFC 9098 is an Informational document published in September 2021 and remains current. It accurately describes the operational reality of IPv6 extension headers in modern networks: they are widely dropped by deployed equipment, limiting their usefulness for protocol extension.

sections.title: The Extension Header Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 is designed to be extended. The specification allows packets to carry optional extension headers that add extra information, such as fragmentation instructions or hop-by-hop processing directives. These headers are meant to be examined and acted upon by the devices that handle the packet.

However, in practice, network devices often drop IPv6 packets that contain extension headers entirely, without ever attempting to process them. This document surveys the reasons why this happens and the implications for IPv6 deployment.

The problem is both technical and operational. Hardware constraints in modern routers make processing extension headers difficult. Security and performance concerns give operators strong reasons to filter them out. And bugs in device implementations of extension header support have made operators wary of allowing them through.
sections.eli5: IPv6 packets can have extra headers, but routers throw them away. This document explains why that happens and why it is hard to fix.

sections.title: How IPv6 Packets Are Structured
sections.content:
IPv4 packets have a fixed-length main header with optional add-ons, specified by an Internet Header Length field. The protocol type comes right after the header.

IPv6 took a different approach: a mandatory fixed 40-byte header, followed by zero or more optional extension headers chained together. Each extension header specifies the type of the next header in the chain. Only after following the entire chain can a device find the actual protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP) and its information.

This linked-list design is more flexible than IPv4, but it creates a fundamental problem: to find and read layer 4 information (like a TCP port or ICMP type), a device must parse every header in the chain, in order. If the extension header chain is long or complex, a router might not be able to process it fast enough to keep up with incoming traffic.
sections.eli5: IPv4 packets have one header, and you know where everything is. IPv6 packets can have a chain of headers, and you have to follow the whole chain to find what you need.

sections.title: Hardware Limitations in Modern Routers
sections.content:
Carrier-grade routers use specialized hardware, such as Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) or Network Processing Units (NPUs), to forward packets at line rate. When deciding where to send a packet, the router copies the first part of the packet (often 192 to 384 bytes) into a lookup engine with special memory like ternary content-addressable memory (TCAM).

There is a trade-off: sending more data to the lookup engine lets the hardware inspect deeper into the packet but reduces the overall forwarding rate. Sending less data keeps the throughput high but limits visibility into the packet.

When a router cannot see far enough into a packet to make a forwarding decision—for example, because extension headers have pushed the layer 4 information beyond its inspection window—the router has few good options. Forwarding the packet anyway might bypass security controls. Punting it to the slow control plane for software processing opens the door to denial-of-service attacks. Dropping it is the safest choice.

Some routers support recirculation, where a packet is looped back through the processing engine multiple times to handle one extension header at a time. However, this approach reduces the router's overall throughput and is not feasible on all hardware architectures.
sections.eli5: Routers look at the first few hundred bytes of a packet to decide where to send it. Extension headers make the packet harder to read, so routers just throw it away.

sections.title: Operational and Security Reasons to Filter
sections.content:
Even if a router had unlimited inspection capability, operators have good reasons to drop extension headers:

Load balancing: When multiple links have equal cost (ECMP), a router hashes layer 3 and layer 4 information to split traffic evenly. Extension headers can hide this information, making load balancing less effective.

Security policies: Networks use access control lists (ACLs) to protect infrastructure and prevent attacks. Layer 4 ACLs are most effective when applied at the network edge. If extension headers hide port numbers or protocol types, the ACL cannot do its job.

Intrusion detection: Intrusion detection and prevention systems (NIDS/IPS) inspect traffic to find attacks. Extension headers increase complexity and can prevent these systems from reading the application-layer traffic they need to analyze.

Firewall evasion: IPv6 extension headers make it trivial to evade security controls designed for the IPv6 header and upper-layer protocol. For example, a device might filter on IPv6 source addresses but miss the same filtering rule when an extension header is inserted between the IPv6 header and the application protocol.

Hop-by-Hop processing: Packets with the Hop-by-Hop Options header are meant to be processed by every router they pass through. However, most implementations send these packets to the control plane (the slower path), which creates a denial-of-service risk. Many operators simply drop these packets.

Implementation bugs: IPv6 extension headers remain poorly tested in practice. Bugs in how different devices parse and process extension headers have been discovered as recently as 2020, even for common implementations.
sections.eli5: Routers need to see port numbers to split traffic fairly. Firewalls need to see port numbers to enforce rules. Extension headers hide those details. Also, routers that do support extension headers have had bugs, so operators prefer to just drop them.

sections.title: Status and Implications
sections.content:
RFC 9098 is an informational document, not a standard. It reflects the operational reality of IPv6 in the public Internet as of 2021.

Extension headers remain defined in the IPv6 specification (RFC 8200), but their practical deployment is limited. Most new features that need to extend IPv6 have moved to other approaches, such as tunneling or options within the application layer. Standards bodies have deprecated some extension headers (like Routing Header Type 0) and advised against others (like atomic fragments).

The document serves as a warning to protocol designers: even if a feature is defined in the IPv6 spec, widespread support cannot be assumed. Any protocol that relies on extension headers needs to provide fallback mechanisms or alternative approaches for networks that filter them.
sections.eli5: This document explains that IPv6 extension headers do not really work on the Internet, so new features should not depend on them. That is still true today.
